text: Exactly. Paid search carries 60 percent of the volume at a .01 rate; the marketplace is small but ugly. Weight by Pr(channel) and you land on .029, which matches the .03 we already had. That agreement is your sanity check.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: The conditional rates are the right inputs; the formula wants Pr(fraud | channel) times Pr(channel). The problem is Boris's weights, not his rates.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: Every order comes in through exactly one of the three, which is what makes them a partition. Nothing is missing — the weighting is what's off.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: No order arrives through two channels at once, so there's no overlap to correct. Look at how the three rates are being combined instead.

speaker: Marcus Odom
text: The vendor's rep sat in my office this morning. Ninety-five percent accurate, he said. Two percent false alarms. Six figures a year.

speaker: Chen Wu
text: Ninety-five percent. So when v2 flags an order, we're ninety-five percent sure it's fraud. That's the slide I'd write.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: That's the slide the vendor would write. Marcus, how rare is fraud on your site?

speaker: Marcus Odom
text: You told me three percent.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: Then hold that thought.\n\nWork it out before Chen builds a deck around the wrong number.

speaker: Boris Kowalski
text: I sliced the flagged orders two ways, device type and account age. Mobile and desktop flag at different absolute counts, so device matters.\n\nAnd since auto-approved and flagged are mutually exclusive, those two are independent — no interaction to model.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: Two claims, both worth checking. Compare the conditional against the prior, the way the handedness survey did it. Counts alone will mislead you.

text: Friday's here. I've got the vendor on the phone at two and a marketplace partner asking me to double my listings.\n\nTell me what a flag is worth, what it costs me to act on one, and whether I'm writing the vendor a check.

speaker: Priya Anand

text: I'll be straight with you. I've had two seasons of people telling me about radians. What I need is: does Jordan swing with a longer club or choke up on the grip? And does Amara's bend technique cost her the race?

text: Both of those are angular kinematics questions, Marcus. You'll get an answer with a number attached to it.

speaker: Coach Marcus Dunbarrow
text: Numbers I can use.

speaker: Tess Alvarez
text: We've got the capture files already open. Joint angles, frame timestamps, segment lengths.

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: Good. Then you two start where we always start, with position and displacement, and we work up to velocity and acceleration. Nothing goes in the memo until you can tell me where each number came from.

speaker: Tess Alvarez
text: Okay, I ran the same thing for the grip point instead of the clubhead and got a smaller number. That can't be right, can it? The grip and the clubhead are on the same shaft. They go through the same swing.

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: They do. Say more about what you think that means.

speaker: Tess Alvarez

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: *(to you)* Go ahead. You just did this calculation twice.

text: Thirty-three metres a second. Fine. So the fix is a longer driver. Order a longer shaft, get a faster clubhead, ball goes further. Why did that take an afternoon?

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: Because that is not the only variable in the equation, and it is not the only thing a longer shaft changes.

speaker: Coach Marcus Dunbarrow
text: Then give me the other option. I'm not buying new equipment on a maybe.

speaker: Tess Alvarez
text: There's the grip thing, right? Like what baseball players do when they choke up on the bat?

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: *(to you)* That's the right instinct, badly explained. You take it.

speaker: Coach Marcus Dunbarrow
text: Alright, I read it. Before I take this to Jordan — tell me in plain language which one of those you'd actually have him try this week, and what I should expect to see.

text: I drafted the bend section already. Want to hear it?\n\n"Amara's centripetal acceleration on the bend is what slows her down. Since she runs at constant speed, there's no acceleration acting on her on the straight, and the centripetal acceleration on the curve is what reduces her speed through the bend. Recommendation: hold the bend wider to cut the centripetal acceleration and keep her speed up."

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: Marcus would sign off on that in about four seconds, which is exactly the problem. Two of those sentences are wrong and one is defensible for the wrong reason.

speaker: Dr. Priya Natarajan
text: One page. Marcus reads the first paragraph and the recommendations and nothing in between, so put the numbers where he'll hit them.\n\nAnd I read the middle. Every recommendation traces to a measurement, or it comes out.

speaker: Coach Marcus Dunbarrow
text: One more. Our baseball staff keeps asking me why their hitters choke up on the bat against a fast pitcher. Same thing you showed me today, or different?

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Mele, congratulations on the promotion. Less fun part: Jamal Reeves. Dunbarrow called me about him twice this week.

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: I know. Tuesday he came in nine minutes after his start and the section wasn't set.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Right. Before you do anything about it, I want you to look at how he was brought on. Who ran his orientation?

text: *(coming in)* Sorry, I heard my name. Mele, he's still inside his three months. We let him go Friday, clean, no notice, no file, no lawyer.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: That's not how we do it here, Dunbarrow.

text: Mele, you're his supervisor, so it's your call to recommend. Build me a file I can stand behind. Two weeks.

text: Jamal, five minutes? Not a discipline thing. I want to know how you were brought on.

text: Rory met me at four, showed me the POS for about ten minutes, gave me an apron, put me on tables 20 through 26 with Priya.

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: Did anyone give you a handbook?

speaker: Jamal Reeves

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: Did you get a job description?

speaker: Jamal Reeves
text: The what?

text: Priya showed me her way. There's a card by the terminal now, I think somebody printed it in May.

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: Has anyone told you how you're being evaluated? Or that you're in a probation period?

speaker: Jamal Reeves
text: No. I figured if I was bad at it, someone would say.

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: And if you had a problem with something here, who would you go to?

speaker: Jamal Reeves
text: Honestly? You, as of last month. Before that, nobody.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Right. A seminar is a method, and you can't pick a method before you know the objective. Jamal's job description is where the objective comes from, not the seminar brochure.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: The trainee isn't really in question here, Dunbarrow named him. What's missing is earlier than that: what the training is supposed to fix, taken from his job description.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: The seminar comes with an instructor, so a trainer technically exists. The step before that is the one nobody did: setting the objective from the job description.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: You're right that nobody has said how we'd know it worked, and that step does get skipped constantly. But it's downstream. With no objective drawn from the job description, there's nothing to measure.

speaker: Jamal Reeves
text: You wanted to see me? I've got table 14 waiting on a dessert order.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Mele. Friday. I've already moved Priya onto his section.

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: I counselled him Tuesday. He's got a follow-up on the 14th.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Counselled. Did you see him on the line Thursday? Full voice at Marco, in front of the pass.

speaker: Mele Fonoti
text: I heard about it. Marco says Jamal told him the ticket was flagged and Marco said it wasn't.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: And Lena thinks a bottle of the Okanagan pinot walked out the week before last.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Thinks, or counted?

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Thinks.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Then it isn't a fact yet, and it doesn't go near his file until somebody investigates it properly.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Susan, he's inside three months. This is the one window where we don't have to do any of this.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: We did do all of this for Reneé last year. Two warnings, a review date, and she's now closing four nights a week.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Reneé had three years in.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Which is a factor. It isn't a different rulebook. Mele, what's your next step?

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Patience isn't neutral here. The behaviour repeated after the counselling and there's a new incident at the pass. Letting the follow-up date do the work leaves us with nothing in the file and nothing changed.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: That's the step. Least severe action that will actually correct it, and it puts the history, the current situation and the consequence on paper where it can be relied on. Draft it today.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Suspension is step three, and we'd be skipping a step we can defend for one we'd have to justify. Before anyone here suspends without pay, we check the provincial employment standards for this situation.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Fine by me, as long as somebody's off the floor.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Thank you.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: No. The probation window makes this legal, not defensible. We followed this process for Reneé on the same behaviour, and consistency is the primary basis for deciding what action to take. Mele, I need the step that matches what we've documented.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Probation ends on the 7th. I want your recommendation in writing before close tonight, and I want it to say Friday.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: It'll say what the file supports, Dunbarrow. Mele, you've got the file. Tell us the step.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: Good. Done.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Mele, walk me through the consistency problem. Reneé got two warnings for the same behaviour, and three years of service was the factor that moved the level, not a different rulebook. And Jamal was never told the standard he's being terminated for missing. The window makes this lawful. It doesn't make it right, and it doesn't make it consistent.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: That's the recommendation the file supports. The least severe action that will correct it, documented, with a review date, and no reliance on the calendar to do our thinking for us.

speaker: Dunbarrow Hayes
text: And if the 14th comes and nothing's changed?

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Then the next step is already written into the warning. That's the point of it.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Suspension skips a step, and before anyone here suspends without pay we check the BC Employment Standards Act for this specific situation. What in the file tells you a written warning won't correct this?

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: Letting the probation date pass is a decision, not a delay, and it's one you'd be making to avoid a conversation. Dunbarrow will notice, and so will Jamal.

speaker: Susan Whitfield
text: File's in front of me. Before I sign it, I want to hear your reasoning in your own words rather than the memo's. Start with this: what would have made Friday the right answer?

speaker: Sergeant Lyle Brennan
text: Michaud. The commander read your file notes on provision 5. We're meeting Nazari at four.

text: The permit's already approved. What's left to discuss?

text: The route, for one. And whether her marshals will hold the line at Harbour and Fifth if the crowd pushes.

text: *(over radio)* Michaud, status on the gap.

speaker: Officer Dana Michaud
text: Two panels down, maybe thirty at the gap, the rest are holding back. Dmitriou's hit, he's walking out.

text: Webb's people are off their gates and moving toward you. I did not send them.

speaker: Officer Dana Michaud
text: Sarge, my ARWEN officers are asking for a direction.

speaker: Sergeant Lyle Brennan
text: Then give them one. I'm four blocks out. You've got the picture, I don't.

text: Thirty people in a crowd of nine hundred and you fired into the mass. Section 25 lets you use a weapon on the person who's the threat. There's no provision anywhere for a weapon on a collective.\n\nVancouver got reviewed for exactly that in 2011 and the ARWEN wasn't even approved for use there. Whatever you thought you were protecting, you just handed every camera on that street the only story they'll run.

speaker: Sergeant Lyle Brennan
text: That's the call. Weapon on the person posing the threat, nobody else, and you keep the line between the gap and the doors.\n\nYou'll get criticized for being too soft — that's one of the two things we always get criticized for. text: Webb's not mine and he's not yours. text: Your officer waved my people off the gap.

speaker: Officer Dana Michaud
text: That's right.

text: I've got a contract that says I secure those three gates. Two panels come down forty metres from Gate 2 and I'm supposed to stand there?

text: You were supposed to stay on your gates, which is what the plan says.

text: My insurer, probably.\n\nLook — I ran a watch for eleven years before this. I'm not the problem you think I am. I just don't have the luxury of being accountable to nine different bodies. I have to meet a payroll every two weeks.

speaker: Officer Dana Michaud

text: I think if Tuesday weren't happening, nobody would be writing it up. Which is the whole question, isn't it.\n\nThe commander's asked for an options paper. speaker: assistant
text: I've read your draft. One suggestion before it goes up. text: The commander's doing a post-event review and she wants a memo from the practicum side. Not a defence of the unit.

speaker: Dana Okafor
text: I've been to four board meetings. I have minutes from all four. In March a cafeteria worker handed my neighbor's eight-year-old a cheese sandwich in front of his class and took his tray away. He has not eaten lunch at school since.

text: Ward County's policy is on their website. Over forty dollars of unpaid balance and the student gets an alternate meal.

speaker: Dana Okafor
text: An alternate meal. A sandwich and a carton of milk, and everyone in line knows what it means. The debt is the parents'. The sandwich goes to the kid.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: How many kids are we talking about in Ward County?

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: Twelve hundred-ish with a balance last year. The district's own numbers.

speaker: Dana Okafor
text: And the next county over writes it off. And the one after that calls parents. Nobody does the same thing, so nobody's accountable for any of it.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: That last part is the part I can use. Dana, I'm not promising you a bill today.

speaker: Dana Okafor
text: I'm not asking for a bill today. I'm asking you to stop telling me it's a district matter.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: *(to you)* All right. Before anything else, write down what the problem actually is and what's causing it. Two different things, and people mix them up constantly. Then tell me who can fix it, because if the answer is the district, Dana's right that we've all been hiding behind that.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: That's the distinction. A single district's policy is a district problem. Twelve different policies and no floor under any of them is a state problem. That's the version I can carry into committee.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: That's the rule of thumb and usually it's the right one — start local and escalate only when local options are exhausted. Dana has been to four board meetings. And the complaint isn't that one district got it wrong, it's that each district does something different. That's the part a board can't fix.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: The commission signs off on dollars. It doesn't write the rule about what happens to a kid at the register. Keep separating who pays from who sets the policy.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: The federal waivers mattered — they're part of why the balances jumped. But waivers expiring isn't something we can reverse from this building, and what happens to a student with a balance is set much closer to home than Washington.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: Before you write "the waivers expired and now kids go hungry" — that's one story. There are at least three others and the association will use all of them.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text:
Household income in the county dropped two years running. That's a poverty story, not a cafeteria story.

Free-meal application rates are down eighteen percent since the waivers ended, and the application is four pages. That's a paperwork story.

And two districts over, the superintendent just writes the debt off. Same waivers, no cold sandwiches. That's a district-discretion story.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: She's not being difficult. Pick the wrong cause and we write a bill that doesn't touch the thing we're angry about. Whoever tells the most convincing cause-and-effect story gets to pick the solution. So pick yours and know why.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: Yes. Same shock, different outcome, so the shock isn't doing the work. Something the district chose is. That's the gap your bill fits into.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: Income explains why balances exist. It doesn't explain why a balance ends with a tray being taken away. Keep those two links apart.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: That one's real and it'd help a bill. But it's still about why families owe money, not about what the district does once they owe it.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: It's a good detail for a hearing. It's not evidence about what causes the substitution — it's evidence about enrollment friction upstream.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: One or two sentences. If the chair can't repeat it back to me after hearing it once, it's too long.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: And give me the name you'd put on it. Not a bill title. The thing people would say out loud.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: Read it to me. I'll be the chair — if I can't say it back to you, it's not done yet.

speaker: Carl Whitfield
text: I read the draft the House member filed last session. I'll save us time: my members don't want kids eating cold sandwiches either.

speaker: Priya Nathan
text: That's a new position.

speaker: Carl Whitfield
text: It's the same position I've had for nineteen years. The sandwich isn't a contract decision, it's a district policy decision, and the senator is about to write a twenty-million-dollar mandate to fix something nineteen superintendents could fix for free on Monday.

speaker: Carl Whitfield
text: So. Tell me what the problem is. Your words, not Ms. Okafor's.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: Carl got to you before I did. Good — better here than in the hearing room.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: And tell me where the issue sits right now and what moves it up. Don't tell me it's important. I know it's important. Tell me what it is and what you want me to do.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: Last thing. I ask every aide this after their first memo.

speaker: Senator Elena Marsh
text: Not what you learned. What you got wrong on Monday and when you noticed.

speaker: Dr. Priya Raman
text: Owen needs a number for Saturday's Sun program, and he needs to know where it came from. That's your week.

text: We've got foil, cardboard, a meter stick, and a forecast that's finally sunny.

text: Hang on. You're going to work out how wide the Sun is with a pin and a piece of foil?

text: With a pinhole, one careful measurement, and some geometry. Owen, tell them what you need.

text: Before you touch any equipment, write down what you already think the answer is. You'll want that later.

text: Screen faces away from the Sun. Foil card goes between the Sun and the screen, and somebody holds the meter stick so the gap stays at 100 centimeters.

text: Write down which of your four numbers you measured, which you picked, and which somebody handed you. Owen will ask.

text: Use 100 million miles for the Sun's distance. The accepted value is nearer 93 million, but a round number keeps your attention on the reasoning rather than on long division.

text: My tracing measured 1.0 centimeter across. Nolan's came out closer to 1.1.

text: Okay, I have to ask. You traced a dot about as wide as my fingernail, and now there's a number on Owen's sign about the actual Sun. What am I missing?

speaker: Hartwell
text: Washer fluid, WF-4L. The system is running two forecasts side by side and planning keeps picking whichever one looked good last month.

text: Dunbarrow signed it. He wants the four-week caveat in the quarterly review notes, which is fair.

text: Ridgeview wants two numbers out of us by Friday. A scholarship cutoff and a support-flag cutoff.

text: And I want to know where those numbers come from. Last year a consultant handed us a cutoff with no explanation.
